items.title: Nursing a Knee Injury: Week Two Update From a Superintendent Who Can't Afford to Be Sidelined
items.targetTitle: One Kilometre at a Time: What a Knee Injury Taught Me About Coming Back to Running
items.anchor: coming back from a knee injury one kilometre at a time
items.insertedSentence: I wrote more about that slow rebuild in [coming back from a knee injury one kilometre at a time](/blog/coming-back-to-running-after-knee-injury).
items.currentContent:
Two weeks in. Still here. Still working. Still limping a little, if I'm being honest, but things are moving in the right direction.

I posted a bit about this when it first happened, so I wanted to follow up. If you've dealt with a lower body injury while working a physically demanding job, you'll probably recognize a lot of what I'm about to say.

## Where Things Stand Right Now

The pain is still there. I'm not going to sugarcoat it. But it's noticeably different from week one. Last week it was sharp and unpredictable, the kind that catches you off guard going down stairs or when you shift your weight the wrong way. This week it's duller, more manageable, and a lot more predictable. I can work around predictable pain. The unpredictable stuff is what gets you into trouble.

I've been icing in the evenings, keeping off it when I can, and being deliberate about how I move through the building during the day. Deliberate is the key word there. I'm not rushing. I'm thinking two steps ahead about whether I actually need to make that trip down to the mechanical room right now or whether it can wait fifteen minutes until I'm already heading that direction anyway.

Small adjustments. They add up.

## The Hard Part About Being a Super With an Injury

Here's the thing about this job that most people outside of it don't fully appreciate, you can't just sit at a desk and power through your day. A superintendent's job is physical, period. You're walking floors, checking mechanical rooms, responding to work orders, hauling garbage bags out of a chute room when your custodian is slammed with something else. The building doesn't stop because your knee is sore.

And I'm not the type to stand around directing traffic while my team does all the physical lifting. That's not how I operate. But I've had to consciously check myself this week, several times, and ask whether I'm about to do something out of habit or ego rather than necessity.

Had a moment midweek where I was about to drop down to help move something heavy and I caught myself. Handed it off. Felt a little weird about it, honestly. But that's the right call and I know it. Pushing through the wrong thing at the wrong time in a recovery is how two weeks becomes six weeks.

## Not Overworking the Knee, But Still Getting the Job Done

I've been leaning on my maintenance worker a bit more than usual for the runs that involve stairs or awkward positions. He knows what's going on and he's been solid. I'm still present, still directing, still signing off on work orders and doing walkthroughs. I'm just being selective about the physical stuff.

The job is getting done. The building is running fine. Nobody would walk in here and know the super is nursing something. That matters to me, not because I'm trying to look tough, but because the residents depend on this place running properly and that doesn't change based on what's going on with me personally.

That said, I'm not playing hero about it either. There's a difference between staying functional and being reckless.

## Looking Ahead to Running Again

I miss running. A lot more than I thought I would after just two weeks. It's become such a regular part of how I decompress and reset that losing it, even temporarily, has a bigger effect than I expected. My wife noticed before I did.

I'm not putting a date on the return yet. That's how you rush it and end up back at square one. But I'm starting to think about it more in practical terms. What does the build-back look like? Walk first. Then short, easy jogs. No hills. No ego about pace. Just reconnecting with the motion before asking anything of the knee.

I've read enough about running injuries to know the return isn't a switch you flip. It's a ramp. And the length of the ramp depends almost entirely on how patient you are now.

I'm working on the patient part.

## What I would do
If you're a superintendent, property manager, or really anyone in a hands-on job dealing with a physical injury right now, the thing I keep coming back to is this: staying functional doesn't mean ignoring what your body is telling you. It means listening closely enough to know what you can still do, what you need to hand off, and where the line is between pushing through and making it worse.

Week two is better than week one. I'll take it.

Check back in next week, either I'm turning a corner or I've got a more interesting story to tell.

items.title: What This Job Is Really Like in Subsidized Housing
items.targetTitle: The Fine Line Between Compassion and Burnout in Working as a Building Superintendent
items.anchor: the fine line between compassion and burnout
items.insertedSentence: That pressure is part of [the fine line between compassion and burnout](/blog/the-fine-line-between-compassion-and-burnout-in-working-as-a-building-superintendent) in this job.
items.currentContent:
Nobody really warned me.

I had experience. I knew buildings. I knew maintenance. I knew how to troubleshoot a problem and when to call a contractor. I thought that meant I had a decent idea of what I was walking into.

I did not.

Subsidized housing has a different weight to it. The building is still a building, but the people inside often carry more than you can see from the hallway. Seniors, people with disabilities, families under stress, people dealing with addiction, people living alone, people who have been through systems most of us only see from the outside.

You are not just walking into a workplace. You are walking into people’s lives.

## The job posting does not explain the real job

The posting usually says maintenance, cleaning, work orders, inspections, tenant service, communication with management.

All true.

What it does not explain is the call from a tenant who has not eaten properly. Or the resident who has not picked up mail all week and something feels wrong. Or the elevator outage that is not just an inconvenience because someone upstairs has a medical appointment and cannot do stairs.

That is the part you learn by being there.

A regular maintenance issue can become a life issue fast. Heat, elevators, water leaks, pests, safety concerns, mental health, hoarding, isolation, family conflict. It all shows up in the building one way or another.

You still have to do the work order. But you also have to understand the person standing in front of you.

## You live in the middle

One of the hardest parts is being between everyone.

Tenants see you as the building person. Management sees you as the person on site. Contractors need access. Staff need direction. Residents need help. And sometimes all of those people want different things at the same time.

You make a lot of judgment calls alone.

Do I escalate this now or watch it for another day? Do I call someone’s emergency contact? Do I push back because the repair is being misunderstood from a desk? Do I step into a hallway argument or let security handle it?

There is no manual for every situation.

You build judgment slowly. Sometimes by getting it right. Sometimes by going home and thinking, I should have handled that differently.

## Old systems make the work harder

The buildings are not the only things that can be old.

Sometimes the tracking systems are old too. Paper notes. Missing history. Work orders that do not tell the whole story. Unit issues that have been around for years but nobody kept clean records.

That matters.

If a unit has repeated mould complaints, water issues, pest issues, or accessibility problems, you need history. Without it, every issue looks brand new. That wastes time and makes it harder to hold anyone accountable.

Even a basic digital record is better than guessing. Dates, photos, notes, follow-ups, vendor reports. Boring stuff, but it protects tenants, staff, and the building.

I care about that more now than I did when I started.

## Boundaries are not optional

This job can pull you in if you let it.

You want to help. Someone is struggling, and you are the person in front of them. It is easy to start carrying things that are not yours to carry.

But you are not a social worker. You are not a therapist. You are not someone’s family. You may have to connect people to those supports, but you cannot become all of them.

That is not cold. That is survival.

Know the resources. Know who to call. Know the emergency contacts, wellness check process, local supports, and escalation steps. Then use them when needed.

A good superintendent cares, but a good superintendent also knows where the line is.

## The good moments are small

People think the big wins are the major repairs. Sometimes they are.

But the moments that stick with me are usually smaller.

A senior who starts saying good morning after months of keeping to herself. A resident who thanks you for listening even though you did not fix anything that day. Someone who reports a problem early because they trust you enough to say something. A floor that slowly starts feeling calmer because people see staff showing up consistently.

Those things matter.

They do not show up neatly in a report, but they change the feeling of a building.

## Why I stay

This job is tiring. Some days it is messy, thankless, and frustrating. Some days you feel like every problem in the building found you at once.

But I stay because I am good at it. I understand the building side, and I care enough about the people side to keep learning it.

You need both.

If you only care about repairs, you miss the human part. If you only care about people and ignore the systems, the building falls apart. The job sits right in the middle.

That is what makes it hard.

That is also what makes it worth doing.

items.title: The Garbage People Leave Behind
items.targetTitle: The Compactor Room Is Not a Magic Hole
items.anchor: why the compactor room is not a magic hole
items.insertedSentence: It connects directly to [why the compactor room is not a magic hole](/blog/why-your-building-garbage-compactor-matters).
items.currentContent:
Illegal dumping always seems to start with one thing.

One mattress beside the bins. One broken chair near the curb. One bag tossed behind a fence because someone did not want to deal with it properly.

Then, almost overnight, it grows.

Another person sees the mattress and thinks, I guess this is where stuff goes now. Then a box shows up. Then construction scraps. Then black garbage bags. Before long, the spot looks abandoned even if people live right beside it.

I have seen this happen around buildings more times than I can count. It is not just ugly. It changes how people treat the space.

## Mess invites more mess

There is something about a dirty area that gives people permission to make it worse.

If the garbage room is clean and the rules are clear, most people behave. Not everyone, but most. If the area already looks neglected, some residents stop caring. They leave things outside the chute. They dump furniture where it does not belong. They walk away from a mess because someone else already started it.

That is one of the reasons building staff jump on dumping quickly. It is not because we enjoy chasing garbage. It is because if we leave it, the problem multiplies.

A mattress left for two days becomes a pile.

## It costs more than people think

People sometimes act like illegal dumping is free.

It is not. Someone pays.

If staff have to drag items out, that is labour time. If a vendor has to remove bulk waste, that is a service cost. If something damages equipment, blocks access, attracts pests, or creates a safety issue, now the cost is bigger. In some cases, the building can also get complaints or fines depending on where the garbage ends up.

And the frustrating part is that a lot of this can be avoided by using the proper bulk pickup process.

Most places have a way to dispose of large items. It might be a scheduled pickup, a designated room, a call-in process, or a drop-off site. It is rarely as convenient as dumping something and walking away, but it is the difference between a normal building operation and a mess everyone has to deal with later.

## It becomes a safety issue fast

Old furniture is one thing. Sharp metal, broken glass, paint cans, electronics, batteries, or renovation debris are another.

I have seen bags rip open with things inside that should never have been placed near regular garbage. I have seen items left where people walk, where kids pass through, or where staff have to reach in and move things by hand.

That is when it stops being only a cleanliness issue.

Now you are talking about cuts, pests, blocked exits, fire risk, and staff getting hurt cleaning up something they should never have had to touch in the first place.

If you would not want your kid, your parent, or your neighbour stepping around it, it probably should not be dumped there.

## Pests do not need an invitation twice

Garbage attracts pests. That is not complicated.

Food waste, leaking bags, open containers, and dumped items give rodents and insects exactly what they need. Once they find a reliable food source, they come back. Then residents start seeing mice, roaches, flies, or worse, and everyone wants the building to fix it immediately.

We can call pest control. We can clean. We can seal gaps. But if people keep feeding the problem with bad disposal habits, the issue keeps coming back.

Garbage control is pest control. People forget that.

## The environment part is real too

I am not going to pretend every dumped couch is an environmental disaster. But some waste absolutely does harm the land and water around us.

Batteries leak. Paint and chemicals seep. Electronics contain materials that should not be sitting in the rain. Garbage near drains can wash into waterways. Animals get into bags and spread waste around.

It all adds up.

The problem with illegal dumping is that it takes something that should be controlled and puts it somewhere nobody is managing it.

That is when small decisions become bigger problems.

## What actually helps

Clear instructions help. Good signage helps. A proper bulk item process helps even more.

People need to know what to do with mattresses, old furniture, electronics, paint, and renovation waste before they are standing there with the item in their hands. If the right option is hard to find, some people will take the lazy option.

Reporting helps too. If you see someone dumping, report it. If you see a pile starting, report it early. Building staff and city crews can deal with one item much faster than a full pile that has been sitting for a week.

And if you are the person getting rid of something, do it properly. Call the pickup line. Use the bulk room. Ask the superintendent. Check the city rules. Whatever the process is, use it.

## It comes down to respect for the place

Garbage tells you a lot about a building.

Not because garbage itself is interesting, but because it shows whether people think the shared space belongs to them or to nobody.

When residents treat the building like nobody owns the problem, staff end up carrying the weight. When people take two extra minutes to dispose of something properly, the building feels different. Cleaner. Safer. Less chaotic.

Nobody is asking for perfection.

Just do not be the person who starts the pile.

items.title: The People Part of Being a Superintendent
items.targetTitle: No, I Can't Read Your Mind: Why Reporting Building Issues Actually Matters
items.anchor: why reporting building issues clearly matters
items.insertedSentence: Good service gets easier when residents understand [why reporting building issues clearly matters](/blog/no-i-cant-read-your-mind-why-reporting-building-issues-matters).
items.currentContent:
Nobody told me how much of this job would be people.

When I first got into building work, I thought the hard part would be mechanical rooms, plumbing calls, cleaning schedules, contractors, keys, inspections, all the normal stuff. And yes, that part matters. You need to know the building. You need to know when something is beyond your scope. You need to know who to call when a system is acting up.

But the part that can make or break your day is usually the conversation in the hallway.

A tenant is upset because a repair is taking too long. Someone is worried because they heard a noise in the wall. Someone else thinks they were forgotten because nobody called them back. Half the time, the issue is not only the repair. It is the feeling that nobody is listening.

That is where a superintendent can either calm the building down or make it worse.

## People want to know they were heard

You do not have to have every answer right away.

If a part is backordered, say that. If a contractor has not confirmed a time yet, say that. If the repair is going to take longer than the tenant wants, be honest about it.

What drives people crazy is silence.

I had a dishwasher leak once where the part took longer than expected. It was not a fun repair. The tenant was annoyed, and honestly, I understood why. But I kept checking in. I told them where things stood. I gave them the timeline I had, not the timeline I wished I had.

When it was finally fixed, they were fine. Not because it was fast. It was not fast. They were fine because they did not feel abandoned.

That is a big difference.

## Do not talk down to people

Tenants do not always understand building systems. Why would they? Most people do not know why a boiler needs maintenance, why a contractor has to inspect before ordering parts, or why a common area repair can take approvals before anything happens.

That does not mean they are stupid.

Explain it in plain language. Do not hide behind technical words. Do not act annoyed because they asked. If someone is frustrated, give them the basic picture: what happened, what you are doing, and when they should expect an update.

That usually solves more than people think.

## Boundaries still matter

Good customer service does not mean being available for every complaint at every hour.

This part is important, especially if you live in or near the building. You can be respectful without letting every hallway conversation turn into a full meeting. You can care about tenants without letting them run your whole day.

If someone catches me when I am in the middle of something, I try not to brush them off. But I also do not let a heated conversation happen in the elevator or lobby if it needs a proper follow-up. Sometimes the best answer is, "Let me look into this and get back to you."

Then you actually have to get back to them.

That last part is where trust is built.

## The difficult tenants still get professionalism

Every building has easy tenants and difficult tenants.

The easy ones say thank you, report issues clearly, and understand that some repairs take time. The difficult ones call three times, escalate quickly, and make every problem feel personal.

You cannot let that change your standard.

You do not have to accept abuse. You do not have to stand there and be yelled at. But you should still be consistent. Same process. Same documentation. Same calm tone. Same follow-up.

If you start playing favourites, people notice. Buildings are small worlds. Word travels.

## Good communication prevents bigger problems

When tenants trust you, they tell you things earlier.

They mention the slow drain before it backs up. They report the hallway light before someone trips. They tell you about a strange smell before it becomes a bigger issue. They give you a heads-up instead of waiting until they are furious.

That makes the job easier.

I have caught problems early because a tenant felt comfortable saying something in passing. That does not happen if people think you do not care or will brush them off.

The relationship matters because the building runs on information.

items.currentContent:
A buddy of mine failed his G test for the second time.

Same issue both times: lane changes on the 401.

He called me after, and I could hear it in his voice. He was not just annoyed. He sounded done. Like he was starting to wonder if maybe driving was just not for him.

I get that feeling. You pay for the test, book the day, take the time, sit there with the examiner beside you, and then one part of the route gets you again. It messes with your confidence.

But failing twice does not mean you are finished.

It means the test found the same weak spot twice.

## Two failures is not the end

In Ontario, your G1 licence is valid for five years. Inside that window, you can attempt the road tests again. There is no magic number where the system says, "Nope, you are done forever."

The real issue is time. If your licence expires before you finish the process, then you can end up starting over. That is the clock you have to respect.

So if you failed twice, do not sit around feeling embarrassed for six months. Take a breath, figure out what went wrong, and train that exact thing.

## The 401 is a different animal

The 401 is not a gentle place to learn confidence.

It is busy, fast, loud, and full of drivers who are not thinking about your road test. Lane changes there require timing, speed control, mirror checks, blind spot checks, and commitment. All at once.

That is where a lot of nervous drivers fall apart.

They check the mirror. Signal. Check again. Look over the shoulder. Then hesitate. The gap starts closing. They slow down a little without meaning to. Now the cars behind them are moving differently. The examiner sees the uncertainty. The driver feels that pressure and the next lane change gets worse.

I have seen that pattern as a passenger.

The problem is not usually that the person knows nothing. The problem is that the move is not automatic yet.

## Practice where the problem happens

This is what I told him: do not book again until you have practiced lane changes on the actual kind of highway that failed you.

Not a quiet road. Not only the DVP if your test keeps putting you on the 401. The 401.

Go with someone calm and experienced. Have them call out lane changes. Left lane when safe. Right lane when safe. Merge. Exit. Re-enter. Do it again. Not once. Not twice. Enough times that your body stops treating it like a crisis.

You are not trying to become fearless. You are trying to become steady.

There is a difference.

## Get one instructor session if you can

A good instructor can spot the exact breakdown faster than a friend can.

Maybe your signal is too late. Maybe your head check is too long and you drift. Maybe you slow down before changing lanes. Maybe you are waiting for a perfect gap that will never come on the 401.

You want someone to tell you the specific mistake.

"Lane changes" is too vague. You need to know which part of the lane change is failing.

One focused lesson before booking again can save you another failed attempt.

If money is tight, even one proper session is better than guessing. Tell the instructor exactly what happened. Do not hide the failed attempts out of embarrassment. That is the information they need.

I would also ask them to run part of the lesson like a mock test. No coaching every second. Just drive, follow instructions, and see what happens when the pressure feels closer to the real thing. Sometimes the skill is there during practice, but the nerves change everything once someone is quietly judging the drive.

That is worth training too.

## Watch the small habits before the lane change

Highway lane changes do not fail only at the moment you move over.

They can fail earlier because your following distance is too tight, your speed does not match traffic, or you are staring in the mirror too long and losing track of what is happening in front of you.

That was one thing I told my friend. Do not treat the lane change like one move. Treat it like a setup. Space first. Speed second. Mirror and blind spot. Then commit when the gap is safe.

If the setup is messy, the lane change feels rushed. If the setup is calm, the move gets easier.

## Do not turn the test into your identity

This is the part I wanted my friend to hear most.

Failing a road test does not mean you are stupid. It does not mean you are hopeless. It does not mean everyone else is better than you.

It means, under test pressure, one skill was not good enough yet.

That is it.

Some people pass on the first try and still drive like they got their licence from a cereal box. Some careful drivers need more attempts because nerves hit them hard. The test is a skills check, not a judgment on your whole life.

## My advice

If you failed twice, do not rush into the third test just to prove something.

Practice the weak spot. Drive the route area if you can. Get one instructor to watch you. Fix the exact habit. Then book again.

And when you are on the highway, do not half-change lanes.

Check. Signal. Look. Match speed. Commit.

The gap will not stay open forever. Take it when it is safe.

items.title: Honesty Builds Trust: Why Character Matters in Building Superintendent Work
items.targetTitle: What This Job Is Really Like in Subsidized Housing
items.anchor: what this job is really like in subsidized housing
items.insertedSentence: That is a big part of [what this job is really like in subsidized housing](/blog/not-all-heroes-wear-capes-superintendent-subsidized-housing-toronto).
items.currentContent:
I found a cellphone a few weeks ago. Nothing dramatic. It was sitting near the pathway leading to the garage, partially tucked against the curb, looked like it had been there for at least a few hours. Newer model, no visible damage. I picked it up, logged it, let my staff know, and then reached out to the superintendents at a few neighbouring buildings in case whoever lost it came knocking somewhere nearby.

Nobody came. The phone eventually made its way through the proper channels.

That's really the whole story. And yet I keep thinking about it, not because it was a big deal, but because it was a small one. And small moments like that are exactly where your character actually gets built.

## This Job Runs on Trust

I've been doing this long enough to know that the technical side of building management, the mechanical systems, the work orders, the preventive maintenance schedules, all of it is learnable. What's harder to teach is the trust that has to exist between you, your staff, your tenants, and the organization you represent.

Tenants let you into their homes. They hand over access to their most personal space based on nothing more than the confidence that you're going to do your job honestly and with integrity. That's not a small thing. I don't take it lightly.

When something goes wrong in a unit, when there's damage, a missing item, a complaint, anything, the first thing that gets tested is whether people believe you. And that belief isn't built in the moment of crisis. It's built in a hundred small moments before the crisis ever arrives.

## What I Actually Tell My Staff

I don't give big speeches. That's not my style. But I'm direct about expectations, and I make those expectations clear early.

If you find something that doesn't belong to you, you report it. If you make a mistake on the job, you tell me before I find out some other way. If a tenant asks you a question and you don't know the answer, you say so and you follow up. Don't guess, don't deflect, don't go quiet.

The found cellphone was a chance to walk the talk in front of my team. I didn't make it a moment. I just handled it the way it should be handled, logged it, communicated it, passed it along properly. But they saw it. That matters more than a policy memo ever would.

## The Quiet Cost of Cutting Corners

I've seen what happens in buildings where that culture doesn't exist. Not pointing fingers at anyone specific, just saying I've worked in enough places and talked to enough colleagues to know that when staff start covering things up, or when a super starts bending rules because "it's easier," the whole operation starts to drift.

A missing item in a unit becomes a he-said-she-said situation. A maintenance mistake that could've been caught early becomes a liability because no one said anything. A tenant who felt dismissed once doesn't forget. And in a government-subsidized housing environment, where tenants are often dealing with real vulnerabilities and have fewer options than most, the stakes of that drift are higher than in a lot of other property types.

This isn't about being perfect. I'm not perfect. But there's a difference between making a mistake and hiding one.

## Respect Doesn't Come From a Title

Being the superintendent doesn't automatically make your staff respect you or your tenants trust you. The title gets you in the room. What you do when you're in there is on you.

I've seen supers who try to manage through authority alone. It doesn't hold. Staff disengage. Tenants work around you instead of with you. You end up spending more energy managing friction than actually running the building.

What actually earns respect, in my experience, is consistency. People want to know what to expect from you. They want to know that if you say something's going to be handled, it gets handled. That if you make a call, it's a fair one. That you're not playing favourites, not cutting corners for convenience, and not pretending you don't see what you clearly see.

The found cellphone wasn't a test of my integrity. It was just a thing that happened. But I think about the version of this job where someone pockets it, tells no one, and moves on. That version of this job costs you something. Maybe nothing immediate. But it costs you something.

## Small Moments, Long Memory

Buildings have long memories, in a way. Tenants talk to each other. Staff notice what you do when you think no one's watching. Colleagues in neighbouring buildings form impressions of how you operate. Your reputation in this profession is built slowly and lost quickly.

I'm not trying to be anyone's moral compass. But I do think that showing up with honesty, even when it's inconvenient, even when it's just a found phone that probably no one would've noticed, is the baseline for doing this job with any real integrity.

It also just makes the job easier. When your staff know you're straight with them, they're straight with you. When tenants trust you, they communicate better and escalate less. When your organization knows you're accountable, you get the autonomy to actually manage your building rather than being micromanaged from above.

Honesty is practical. In this profession, it's one of the most practical things you've got.

## What I would do
The next time something small lands in front of you, a found item, a minor mistake, a situation where the easier path is to say nothing, ask yourself what the right call is. Then make it. Not because anyone's watching. Because that's the job.

items.title: Why Your Underground Parking Garage Is Not a Storage Unit
items.targetTitle: The Scooter in the Middle of the Hallway
items.anchor: the scooter in the middle of the hallway
items.insertedSentence: It is the same shared-space problem I saw with [the scooter in the middle of the hallway](/blog/scooters-in-hallway-problem).
items.currentContent:
I get it. The parking spot feels like your space. You pay for it, you use it every day, and that corner next to your car seems like a perfectly reasonable place to stash a spare tire or leave that old bookshelf you haven't gotten rid of yet. I've heard every version of this reasoning over the years.

But here's the thing, underground parking garages are shared infrastructure. They're not extensions of your unit. And the stuff people leave down there creates problems that go way beyond a messy-looking garage.

## What I Actually See Down There

In my experience, the clutter builds up gradually. It starts with one spare tire. Then someone else leaves a stroller they only use seasonally. Then a bike with a flat tire that's been sitting for eight months. Then boxes, then a broken shelving unit, then furniture someone was "about to" donate.

Before long, you've got a parking garage that looks more like a storage locker explosion. And every single one of those items is now someone else's problem, usually mine.

Had a situation once where a set of old patio furniture was left wedged between two parking stalls. Nobody claimed it. Nobody moved it. It sat there through an entire winter, and when spring came around, it had shifted enough to partially block the fire access lane. That's not a minor inconvenience. That's a liability.

## The Fire Hazard Problem Is Real

This is the one I really want people to understand. Underground parking garages already have a complex fire safety setup, sprinkler systems, fire doors, ventilation designed to manage smoke, clearly marked exit routes. When you start stacking furniture and boxes and rubber tires in corners and along walls, you are directly interfering with how that system is supposed to work.

Tires are highly flammable. Upholstered furniture is highly flammable. Cardboard boxes are highly flammable. A fire in a parking garage is already one of the worst-case scenarios for a residential building, and stored combustibles make it significantly worse.

Fire inspectors in Toronto don't take this lightly either. I've seen buildings get dinged on inspections specifically because of tenant items left in parking areas. That becomes a building-wide issue, for the owner, the property manager, and ultimately the other residents who did nothing wrong.

## Emergency Access Is Not Optional

Fire lanes, exit paths, and access routes in a parking garage are measured and planned very deliberately. There's a reason the lines are painted where they are. Emergency responders need to be able to move through a building quickly, with equipment, in low visibility, under pressure.

A stroller left in the wrong spot sounds like nothing. A folded-up exercise bike leaning against a wall sounds like nothing. But in the middle of a fire evacuation or a medical emergency at 2am, obstacles like that can slow everything down. In emergency response, seconds matter. I've thought about that a lot over the years.

The other thing people don't consider is accessibility. Not everyone in a building can easily step around or navigate past clutter. Residents with mobility aids, people carrying young children, older tenants, they all use the parking garage and the pathways leading from it. Clutter doesn't just block emergency access. It creates daily barriers for real people trying to get in and out of their own building.

## Why This Makes My Job Harder (And Why That Matters)

I want to be honest here. The enforcement side of this is exhausting. Posting notices, tracking down who owns what, waiting for responses, escalating to property management, arranging disposal, it's a whole process for every single item. And it's a process that repeats itself constantly because as soon as one thing gets removed, something else appears.

What I tell tenants is simple: I'm not out to get you. I'm not doing this to be difficult. But my job is to keep this building safe and operational for everyone in it, and that means I can't look the other way when shared spaces get treated like personal storage.

When clutter becomes a pattern, it also breeds resentment between tenants. The person whose walkway is blocked is annoyed. The person who parks next to the pile of junk is annoyed. It affects how people feel about the building they live in.

## Where Your Stuff Should Actually Go

Most buildings have designated storage lockers for a reason. If yours came with one, use it. If you've outgrown it, that's the signal to reassess what you're keeping, not to expand into shared space.

For seasonal items like winter tires, there are tire storage services in Toronto that are reasonably priced and take the whole headache away. Strollers belong in your unit or your locker. Furniture you're not using anymore needs to either go into storage, be donated, or be disposed of properly, not parked in a garage corner indefinitely.

Large item disposal in the city has options. Toronto's bulk item pickup, donation drop-offs, Facebook Marketplace, there are ways to deal with things that don't involve leaving them in a shared space and hoping nobody notices.

## The Bottom Line

The parking garage is a shared space that serves a safety function, a practical function, and an operational function all at once. It's not overflow storage. It's not a place to deal with later. It's a space that needs to stay clear so that everyone, including you, can get out safely if something goes wrong.

If you're a tenant reading this, take a walk down to your parking spot this week and look honestly at what's there. If it's not your car, it probably shouldn't be there.

If you're a property manager or building owner, clear signage, regular walkthroughs, and consistent enforcement are your best tools. The cost of dealing with clutter proactively is a lot lower than the cost of an incident that could have been prevented.

Keep the lanes clear. Keep the exits clear. It's one of the simplest things we can do to protect the people living in these buildings.

I get it. The parking spot feels like your space. You pay for it, you use it every day, and that corner next to your car seems like a perfectly reasonable place to stash a spare tire or leave that old bookshelf you haven't gotten rid of yet. I've heard every version of this reasoning over the years.

But here's the thing, underground parking garages are shared infrastructure. They're not extensions of your unit. And the stuff people leave down there creates problems that go way beyond a messy-looking garage.

## What I Actually See Down There

In my experience, the clutter builds up gradually. It starts with one spare tire. Then someone else leaves a stroller they only use seasonally. Then a bike with a flat tire that's been sitting for eight months. Then boxes, then a broken shelving unit, then furniture someone was "about to" donate.

Before long, you've got a parking garage that looks more like a storage locker explosion. And every single one of those items is now someone else's problem, usually mine.

Had a situation once where a set of old patio furniture was left wedged between two parking stalls. Nobody claimed it. Nobody moved it. It sat there through an entire winter, and when spring came around, it had shifted enough to partially block the fire access lane. That's not a minor inconvenience. That's a liability.

## The Fire Hazard Problem Is Real

This is the one I really want people to understand. Underground parking garages already have a complex fire safety setup, sprinkler systems, fire doors, ventilation designed to manage smoke, clearly marked exit routes. When you start stacking furniture and boxes and rubber tires in corners and along walls, you are directly interfering with how that system is supposed to work.

Tires are highly flammable. Upholstered furniture is highly flammable. Cardboard boxes are highly flammable. A fire in a parking garage is already one of the worst-case scenarios for a residential building, and stored combustibles make it significantly worse.

Fire inspectors in Toronto don't take this lightly either. I've seen buildings get dinged on inspections specifically because of tenant items left in parking areas. That becomes a building-wide issue, for the owner, the property manager, and ultimately the other residents who did nothing wrong.

## Emergency Access Is Not Optional

Fire lanes, exit paths, and access routes in a parking garage are measured and planned very deliberately. There's a reason the lines are painted where they are. Emergency responders need to be able to move through a building quickly, with equipment, in low visibility, under pressure.

A stroller left in the wrong spot sounds like nothing. A folded-up exercise bike leaning against a wall sounds like nothing. But in the middle of a fire evacuation or a medical emergency at 2am, obstacles like that can slow everything down. In emergency response, seconds matter. I've thought about that a lot over the years.

The other thing people don't consider is accessibility. Not everyone in a building can easily step around or navigate past clutter. Residents with mobility aids, people carrying young children, older tenants, they all use the parking garage and the pathways leading from it. Clutter doesn't just block emergency access. It creates daily barriers for real people trying to get in and out of their own building.

## Why This Makes My Job Harder (And Why That Matters)

I want to be honest here. The enforcement side of this is exhausting. Posting notices, tracking down who owns what, waiting for responses, escalating to property management, arranging disposal, it's a whole process for every single item. And it's a process that repeats itself constantly because as soon as one thing gets removed, something else appears.

What I tell tenants is simple: I'm not out to get you. I'm not doing this to be difficult. But my job is to keep this building safe and operational for everyone in it, and that means I can't look the other way when shared spaces get treated like personal storage.

When clutter becomes a pattern, it also breeds resentment between tenants. The person whose walkway is blocked is annoyed. The person who parks next to the pile of junk is annoyed. It affects how people feel about the building they live in.

## Where Your Stuff Should Actually Go

Most buildings have designated storage lockers for a reason. If yours came with one, use it. If you've outgrown it, that's the signal to reassess what you're keeping, not to expand into shared space.

For seasonal items like winter tires, there are tire storage services in Toronto that are reasonably priced and take the whole headache away. Strollers belong in your unit or your locker. Furniture you're not using anymore needs to either go into storage, be donated, or be disposed of properly, not parked in a garage corner indefinitely.

Large item disposal in the city has options. Toronto's bulk item pickup, donation drop-offs, Facebook Marketplace, there are ways to deal with things that don't involve leaving them in a shared space and hoping nobody notices.

## The Bottom Line

The parking garage is a shared space that serves a safety function, a practical function, and an operational function all at once. It's not overflow storage. It's not a place to deal with later. It's a space that needs to stay clear so that everyone, including you, can get out safely if something goes wrong.

If you're a tenant reading this, take a walk down to your parking spot this week and look honestly at what's there. If it's not your car, it probably shouldn't be there.

If you're a property manager or building owner, clear signage, regular walkthroughs, and consistent enforcement are your best tools. The cost of dealing with clutter proactively is a lot lower than the cost of an incident that could have been prevented.

It is the same shared-space problem I saw with [the scooter in the middle of the hallway](/blog/scooters-in-hallway-problem).

Keep the lanes clear. Keep the exits clear. It's one of the simplest things we can do to protect the people living in these buildings.

items.title: My First Acupuncture Treatment: What a Running Injury Taught Me About Stretching and Recovery
items.targetTitle: One Kilometre at a Time: What a Knee Injury Taught Me About Coming Back to Running
items.anchor: coming back from a knee injury one kilometre at a time
items.insertedSentence: This was part of the same recovery arc as [coming back from a knee injury one kilometre at a time](/blog/coming-back-to-running-after-knee-injury).
items.currentContent:
I run. Not competitively, not even consistently, but I run. It clears my head after long days in the building, after dealing with maintenance calls and tenant concerns and all the little fires that come with this job. Running is my reset button. So when my knees started talking back to me, I didn't love what they had to say.

The pain crept in slowly. A bit of soreness after a run here, some stiffness the next morning there. I kept going. Classic mistake. Eventually I had to stop and face the obvious: something was wrong, and ignoring it wasn't working.

## The Physiotherapist Didn't Let Me Off Easy

I booked a session with my physiotherapist, expecting her to confirm I had a "minor thing" and send me home with some ice packs. That's not what happened.

She evaluated my knees thoroughly and got straight to the point. I wasn't stretching enough before my runs. Actually, scratch that, I was barely stretching at all. She explained what that actually does to your muscles, and it stuck with me.

When you don't stretch before exercise, your muscles go into the activity cold and tight. They're not prepared for the load you're about to put on them. Over time, those tight muscles pull unevenly on tendons and joints. The knee is a complicated joint, it's not designed to absorb repeated impact when the surrounding muscles are chronically short and stiff. She described it almost like pulling on a rope that's already fraying. Eventually something gives.

That visual hit home. I've been doing this to myself every run.

## So She Suggested Acupuncture

I'll be transparent here. My first instinct was skepticism. I'm a tech person at heart, I like things I can measure and explain. Needles in specific points on your body affecting pain somewhere else? I wasn't immediately sold.

But I trust my physiotherapist, and she explained the reasoning before we started. Acupuncture works by stimulating specific points in the body, in my case, around the knee and the surrounding muscle groups. The stimulation encourages blood flow to the area, helps release muscle tension, and triggers the body's own pain-relief response. It also interrupts the pain signal loop that forms when an area has been irritated for a while. She's used it on athletes, on older clients with chronic joint issues, and on people like me who just pushed a little too hard without the right prep work.

She was calm about it. Matter-of-fact. "Let's try this and see how your body responds."

## The Actual Treatment

She had me lie down and placed several fine needles around my knee and into specific points on my leg. I won't pretend there's zero sensation, there is. But it's not what you're probably imagining. It's a mild pressure, sometimes a subtle ache or warmth around the needle site. Nothing sharp, nothing alarming.

I focused on breathing. She left the needles in for a set period while I just... rested. That part I didn't mind at all, honestly. Between running the building and everything else, lying still for twenty minutes felt like a luxury.

When she removed the needles, I sat up slowly. And here's the part I wasn't expecting: I immediately felt a difference. Not dramatic, not like someone flipped a switch, but the tension around my knee had noticeably softened. There was a lightness there that hadn't been there when I walked in. I moved my leg around and the stiffness that had been greeting me all week was quieter.

I wasn't ready to go sprint around the block. But I felt genuinely better.

## What I'm Doing Between Sessions

My physiotherapist didn't just send me home with a positive feeling and call it done. She gave me a plan for managing things between treatments.

I've been wearing a knee brace during any activity. I resisted this for a while because it felt like admitting defeat, but it's been helpful. It keeps the joint supported and reminds me not to overdo it. Good tool. No shame in using it.

I've also been using a massager on the affected area, working through the muscle around the knee, not just on the knee itself. The soreness lives in the muscles too, not just the joint, and hitting those surrounding areas has helped keep things loose between sessions.

And stretching. Yes. Finally. I've started doing it properly before and after every run. Quads, hamstrings, calves, hip flexors. The full picture. My physiotherapist walked me through which stretches actually matter for knee health, and I've been consistent about it. It takes maybe eight to ten minutes. I spent years skipping eight to ten minutes and paying for it with weeks of recovery. That math doesn't work.

## What I'd Tell Anyone Who's Curious About Acupuncture

Don't let the needles be the thing that stops you from trying it. I've seen people manage chronic pain, tight muscles, and slow-healing injuries with acupuncture as part of a broader treatment plan. My experience was one session, one very noticeable result. That doesn't mean it's a cure-all, it's one tool in the recovery toolkit, and it works best alongside proper physiotherapy guidance.

The bigger lesson for me, honestly, is the stretching one. I've spent years being active without doing the maintenance. That's like running a building and skipping all the preventive maintenance, eventually something breaks, and the repair costs more than the prevention ever would have.

## What I would do
If you're a runner, or honestly anyone who's physically active and skipping the warm-up, book a session with a physiotherapist before an injury forces you to. Don't wait until your knees are telling you to stop. Ask about your stretching habits, ask about your recovery routine, and if acupuncture comes up as a suggestion, give it a real chance. Go in with an open mind, listen to what your body does afterward, and combine it with the basics: supportive gear if you need it, regular massage on tight areas, and actual stretching before you move.

Your body keeps score. Might as well give it a fighting chance.

items.title: The Fine Line Between Compassion and Burnout in Working as a Building Superintendent
items.targetTitle: The People Part of Being a Superintendent
items.anchor: the people part of being a superintendent
items.insertedSentence: A lot of that starts with [the people part of being a superintendent](/blog/customer-service-building-superintendent-why-it-matters).
items.currentContent:
Nobody tells you this part when you take the job.

They talk about mechanical systems, emergency response, work orders, unit inspections. They cover the physical side, the long days, the fact that a pipe doesn't care that it's 3 p.m. on a Friday. That stuff I understood going in. I signed up for it.

What I didn't fully understand, what I don't think you can fully understand until you're living it, is the human weight this work carries. Especially in subsidized housing. Especially when you're the person who's just... there. Every single day.

## You Become the Constant

In a building like mine, a lot of residents don't have a stable network around them. Some of them have family, some don't. Some have support workers who come and go, case managers who rotate, services that get cut or rescheduled. But I'm here. Monday through Friday, 8 to 4:30, and residents know that. They know my face. They know my name. They know I'll answer if they knock.

That consistency matters to people. I've come to understand that. And most days I think it's one of the genuinely meaningful parts of this job, that just showing up, being reliable and decent, actually does something for people who haven't always had that.

But it also means you hear things. You see things. You notice when someone who's usually chatty goes quiet for a week, or when a resident who's been doing well starts looking like they're not sleeping. You pick up on it because you're paying attention, and you pay attention because you care.

And caring, over time, is expensive.

## The Stuff That's Not in the Work Order

I had a resident knock on the office door once, not for a maintenance issue. Just to talk. They'd had a bad night. They were scared. They didn't have anyone else to call at that hour, and they knew I'd be in the next morning.

I sat with them for a bit. I listened. I pointed them toward the right supports and made sure they were okay before I got back to my day.

That's not in any job description I've ever read. But I'd do it again tomorrow. Most superintendents I know would.

The problem isn't the individual moments. The problem is what happens when those moments accumulate, when you're absorbing pieces of other people's hardest days, week after week, and there's no real outlet for it. No debrief. No supervision in the clinical sense. Just you, driving home, replaying a conversation and wondering if you said the right thing or missed something you should have caught.

## The Guilt of the Boundary

Here's what I find hard to admit: sometimes I don't want to hear it.

Not because I don't care. I do. But there are days when I've already had a difficult morning, I've got three work orders stacking up, and someone wants to pull me into something heavy that I genuinely am not equipped to handle. Not my role. Not my training. And I know the right move is to redirect them to the proper supports, to be kind but clear about what I can and can't do.

I know that. I do it.

And then I feel guilty about it for the rest of the afternoon.

That guilt is something I wasn't prepared for. The second-guessing. The wondering if I was cold, or unhelpful, or whether the person actually got the support they needed after I redirected them. There's no follow-up report that lands on my desk confirming everything turned out fine. You just move on and hope.

## What It Does to You Over Time

I don't think I'm burned out. But I've had stretches where I could feel the edge of it.

There's a version of this job where you stop feeling things because it's the only way to get through the day. I've seen that in other superintendents, a kind of flatness that sets in. They're not bad at the job. They're just done caring and they haven't quit yet. That worries me more than anything else about this line of work.

Because the caring is also what makes you good at it. If you stop noticing the person behind the work order, you start missing things. You lose the instinct that tells you something's off before it becomes a crisis. The human attentiveness and the professional attentiveness are connected in this environment. You can't fully separate them.

So the question I keep sitting with, and I don't have a clean answer, is how you stay open enough to be effective without staying so open that you're hollowed out by it.

## The Part Nobody Talks About in Property Management Circles

I go to the occasional industry event, read the trade publications, sit in on webinars sometimes. The conversation is almost always operational. Systems, compliance, capital planning, vendor management. All of it necessary. None of it touches this.

There's almost no space in professional housing circles to talk about the emotional reality of the work. Especially for superintendents, who are kind of caught in the middle, not senior management, not social services, but expected to hold a building full of people together while staying squarely in our lane.

That silence doesn't mean other supers aren't feeling it. It just means nobody's saying it out loud.

I'm not sure why I'm saying it now, exactly. Maybe because I had a hard week and I needed to put it somewhere. Maybe because I think there's someone else reading this who's been carrying the same thing and wondering if they're the only one.

You're not.

Some days I manage the balance well. Some days something follows me home and parks itself at the dinner table. My wife has heard more than her share of anonymized building stories over the years, and I'm grateful she's patient with it.

But I don't have a framework for it. I don't have three steps. I'm just a person doing a job that matters, trying not to lose something in the process that I won't easily get back.

That's where I am with it.
